The software usability shall be low-ambiguity.
Learnability should be supported outside the flight software itself through procedures, onboard limits, and ground system tools that present status in a consistent way.
The support materials for new team members or operators should include operator manuals, command dictionaries, anomaly response guides, and mission-specific training runs or simulations.
The flight software should be predictable and provide clear feedback to help with onboarding.
Documentation and rehearsed operations should provide the main onboarding support.
The system shall avoid ambiguity when the system changes mode or crosses a version boundary.
The flight software shall keep internal data structures versioned.
The flight software shall validate any stored state before using it.
When a mode change occurs, the system shall reconcile pending command state, detector configuration, and housekeeping values.
The system shall prevent the instrument from starting from a partially applied setup or carrying forward corrupted context after a mode change.
The event stream and status reporting should align directly with the ground displays and the operator procedures.
A new person should be able to read a message and find the same term, state, or expected action in the documentation.
The ground tools should surface the flight software’s codes and events in a human-readable way.
The manuals or checklists should explain what each common event means.
The manuals or checklists should explain what normal follow-up looks like.
The manuals or checklists should explain which events require escalation.
The system should help operators learn the same vocabulary they will use in operations.
The feedback should stay tied to a documented response path to support day-to-day missions.
The software shall treat any onboard transition as a controlled handoff rather than implicitly reusing old data.
If the format or version does not match what was expected, the software shall preserve the prior valid state and flag the condition to ground instead of trying to guess.
The software shall make transitions atomic from its point of view.
Transitions must be explainable after the fact when delayed ground contact and limited onboard visibility are present.
The system shall use explicit event logging.
The system shall use version tagging.
The system shall maintain a clear trail of what was active, what was converted, and where the process stopped when something odd happens.
Operational procedures shall keep transitions simple and reversible rather than trying to do too much in one step.
The flight software shall use staged updates during transitions.
The flight software shall check compatibility up front before applying a transition.
Every command path, mode change, and fault response shall be visible in the logs and traceable back to a requirement and a verification result.
The software shall record enough context about who issued the command, the state it was in, whether it was accepted or deferred, and the final outcome.
The system shall allow operators and engineers to reconstruct events later from the recorded context.
With delayed ground contact, the system shall make the safe choice onboard first and rely on the audit trail afterward to prove what happened and why.
Every significant action shall be authorized before execution.
The software shall provide careful state reporting so that exactly what changed and when can be determined.
The flight software shall report transition outcomes beyond a generic "mode changed" or "version loaded" status.
